clue.text: It’s uttered very briefly on weird social media, initially (8)

indicators.note: Briefly asks for the short form of the word beside it, and the shortest form a word can have is its recognised single-letter abbreviation.
Weird means out of the ordinary shape, so the letters beside it will not stand in the ordinary order they arrive in.
Initially points at the start of a word, so only the letter that opens it is taken.

blocks.note: V is the everyday shortening of very, as in a school report's 'v good'
six letters resettled into a new order
the opening letter of the word, taken on its own

explanation.surface: A rumour going round briefly on some strange corner of social media.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social media' is one modern phrase and the clue splits it in two, taking one word for its letters and the other for its initial.
explanation.definitionFit: Vocalism is sound made with the voice, the exercise of the vocal organs, so the definition names a thing the voice produces.

clue.text: Eye problem from middle of last year (4)

indicators.note: The middle of a written phrase is what survives when you bite an equal amount off each end, so the phrase is measured rather than read.

blocks.note: eight letters run together, and the two at each end are dropped

explanation.surface: An eye complaint carried over from halfway through last year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle of last year' reads as a date, somewhere around June, and that is the whole disguise: it points at the centre of a phrase, not at a month.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is the small painful swelling that comes up on an eyelid, which is a problem of the eye rather than of sight.

clue.text: Seaweed gourmet ultimately put on fish (6)

indicators.note: Ultimately means at the very end, so what is taken from the word beside it is the letter that finishes it.
Putting one thing on another rests it on top, and in a down entry the top is where the letters begin.

blocks.note: the last letter of the word, taken on its own
to angle is to fish with rod and line

explanation.surface: A food writer's last word on seaweed, laid over a fish course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' is the verb, not the animal, which is where the clue is hardest: everything around it is edible, so you read it as a thing on a plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Tangle is the name coastal Britain gives to the broad-fronded kelp that washes up on beaches, so the definition is the plant's plain name.

clue.text: Problem pupil stimulated in a communal meeting (8)

indicators.note: In means inside, so the piece named before it is planted within the letters that follow rather than laid beside them.

blocks.note: a bee is a gathering of neighbours for a shared job — a quilting bee, a spelling bee — and with the clue's own 'a' in front the letters part to make room
to be sent is to be carried away with excitement, as in music that really sends you

explanation.surface: A troublemaker at school getting worked up at some village get-together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent' for thrilled is jazz slang and is the step most solvers stall on. The surface's problem pupil is present and misbehaving, which is exactly the opposite of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An absentee is the one who is not there, so in a school register the definition names the pupil by the trouble the empty seat causes.

clue.text: Radicals assuming rising changes image (10)

indicators.note: What rises travels upwards, and a down answer read upwards takes the letters of that piece from the bottom of the grid to the top.

blocks.note: assuming a thing is supposing it, the job the little word 'if' does, and its two letters are read from the bottom up
a company that changes its public image rebrands

explanation.surface: Radicals reckoning that an uprising will change how they are seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assuming rising' reads as one idea, revolutionaries counting on an uprising, and it is really two instructions: a three-letter conjunction and an about-turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A firebrand is an agitator who stirs people up, so the plural sits straight in for radicals in the political sense.

clue.text: Wide open spaces since found, after a journey over river (6)

indicators.note: Something found after a thing comes along behind it, so this piece is parked at the end of everything the rest has built.
A piece written over another stands above it, and in a down entry standing above means coming first.

blocks.note: the clue's own word, taken as it stands
a go is a turn or spell at something, as in having a go
R is the map-maker's short form for river
as means since in the causal sense — as it was raining, we stayed in

explanation.surface: Broad empty country discovered at the end of a trip across a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Every piece here is two letters or fewer, so there is nothing solid to grip: the clue is assembled from four scraps in a different order from the one it reads in.
explanation.definitionFit: The agora was the public square of a Greek city, the market and meeting ground, so the plural names open spaces at the heart of a town.

clue.text: Make short counterargument with pamphlet (8)

blocks.note: the con is the case against, the other half of the pros and cons
a tract is a short printed pamphlet, usually arguing a religious or political case

explanation.surface: Boiling down an objection and issuing it as a pamphlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make short counterargument' reads as one instruction — abridge the objection — and that is the trap: the definition stops dead after two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To contract something is to draw it in so that it takes up less room, which is making it short as a verb.

clue.text: Subject embracing monarch in global circle (6)

indicators.note: An embrace closes right round whatever is held, so the word doing it opens up and takes the next letter inside.

blocks.note: the subject under discussion is the topic, and the word parts after its first letter
R is rex or regina, the letter a monarch signs after the name

explanation.surface: A subject of the Crown who holds his monarch dear the world over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subject' is the word being talked about, not a citizen, and the surface leans hard the other way by putting a monarch next to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cancer and Capricorn are each a line of latitude drawn right round the earth, so the definition names one of them by its shape on the globe.

clue.text: Part of ship that crosses river, often (6)

blocks.note: the raised deck with the wheel and the windows, where the officer of the watch stands
the structure that carries a road or a railway over water — though plenty of them span roads, valleys and railways instead, which is what 'often' admits

explanation.surface: One part of a ship, described as the bit that usually gets you over the water.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Part of ship that crosses river' as a single phrase and you are hunting for a hull or a ferry. The clue is two definitions laid end to end, and the join is invisible.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's bridge is the raised platform the vessel is steered from; the other kind carries a road or railway from bank to bank.

clue.text: Cold primate in sleeveless cloak (4)

blocks.note: C is the letter on the cold tap and on a weather chart
the zoological order, and its best-known member

explanation.surface: A shivering monkey wrapped up in a cloak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' is the setter's favourite double meaning: an archbishop is a primate too, and an ecclesiastical garment is exactly what the definition sounds like it is heading for.
explanation.definitionFit: A cape is the short cloak that hangs from the shoulders with no sleeves at all, so the definition describes the garment exactly.

clue.text: Kind of fool whose company isn’t wanted? (10)

blocks.note: a fool is the pudding of crushed fruit folded into cream, and this is the sharp green fruit that makes the classic one
the third person trailing after a courting couple who would rather be alone, an idiom every British solver grows up with

explanation.surface: An idiot nobody can bear to spend an evening with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool' is the trap and it is a good one: it reads as an insult and it is a dessert, so the whole first half of the clue means something other than it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: Gooseberry fool is a real pudding, so 'kind of fool' defines by example; and to play gooseberry is to be the unwanted third with a couple.

clue.text: In some clues, I’m pleasantly straightforward (6)

indicators.note: Saying you need only some of what follows, and that it is in there, points at a run of letters already written out rather than at a whole word.

blocks.note: six consecutive letters run from the end of the first word, across the second and into the third

explanation.surface: The setter promising that at least some of today's clues will be kind to you.
explanation.walkthrough: Brendan is talking about his own puzzle, which is why the sentence reads so naturally that you never count its letters. The apostrophe carries no instruction at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Something simple has nothing complicated about it, which is the everyday sense of straightforward applied to a task or an explanation.

clue.text: What helps reproduce stock, say? Pet bull one redeployed (6,4)

indicators.note: Redeploying troops sends them to new positions, so these letters take up different places from the ones they start in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A farmer moving his prize bull about to get the herd in calf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stock' is the scented garden flower here, not livestock, and 'say' marks it as one example of a plant — which is what makes the cattle-breeding surface so convincing.
explanation.definitionFit: A pollen tube grows down from a grain to deliver the male cells that fertilise a flower, so it is what lets a plant like stock breed.

clue.text: Present setter’s anagram to intrigue (8)

indicators.note: The word names the device outright: whatever letters stand beside it are to be re-sorted, and here it hides by being something a setter would genuinely be presenting.

blocks.note: someone present is in, the word a register or a receptionist uses
six more letters of the fodder, the possessive doing nothing but joining them on

explanation.surface: The setter offering up an anagram in the hope of tempting you in.
explanation.walkthrough: Naming the device out loud is the disguise. A setter presenting an anagram is an ordinary thing to say, so the instruction reads as scenery instead of an order.
explanation.definitionFit: To interest somebody is to catch and hold their curiosity, which is what intrigue means as a verb.

clue.text: Poet’s one line in masculine style (6)

indicators.note: In puts what comes before it inside what comes after, so the two single letters are planted between the pieces named next.

blocks.note: M is the standard abbreviation for masculine
I is one in Roman numerals
L is the usual short form of line
ton, borrowed from the French, is style or fashionable society — the Regency's word for the smart set

explanation.surface: A poet managing a single line in a thoroughly manly manner.
explanation.walkthrough: Three of the four pieces are single letters, so almost nothing here is a word: the clue is assembled letter by letter and only the last chunk is worth learning.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton wrote Paradise Lost, so 'Poet' names the answer as one instance of the trade rather than defining the word.

clue.text: Supplier of drug mostly impounded, destroyed (5,3)

indicators.note: Mostly means all but a little, and the little you leave off a written word is the letter at the end of it.
Something destroyed has been broken up, so its letters do not survive in the order they were given.

blocks.note: the word gives up its final letter, leaving eight to be broken up

explanation.surface: Most of a dealer's stock seized by the police and then burnt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supplier of drug' reads as a dealer, a person, and the answer is a room. The surface's seizure keeps you looking for someone to arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: An opium den is the establishment where the drug was sold and smoked, so 'supplier' names a place rather than a person.

clue.text: Economist making crucial point inconclusively (6)

indicators.note: What is done inconclusively stops short of the end, so the word it applies to never reaches its final letter.

blocks.note: the key point in an argument is the crucial one
a ness is a headland, the point of land that runs out into the sea, as in Sheerness — and its last letter never arrives

explanation.surface: An economist making a vital point and not quite clinching it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' in a crossword is usually a compass direction, N or S or E or W, and that expectation is what hides the coastal sense the clue actually wants.
explanation.definitionFit: John Maynard Keynes is the economist who argued that governments should spend their way out of a slump, so the bare word names him by his trade.

clue.text: Relinquish or keep subscribing? (4,4)

blocks.note: what you do to a right or a property by putting your name at the bottom of a form
to subscribe is literally to write your name underneath, and keeping at anything is doing it away

explanation.surface: A choice between giving something up and carrying on paying for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Away' does two entirely different jobs: in the first sense it carries the rights off for good, and in the second it means without pause, as in work away or chatter away.
explanation.definitionFit: To sign away a right is to surrender it by putting your name to a document; and since 'away' can mean incessantly, it also reads as going on signing.

clue.text: Free traitor imprisoned by US troops (6)

indicators.note: Being imprisoned by somebody puts you inside their walls, so the piece named first is shut in by the letters that follow.

blocks.note: American soldiers are GIs, from the government issue stamped on their kit, and the word opens after its first letter
a rat is the informer who sells his own side

explanation.surface: A turncoat locked up by the Americans and then let go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free' opens the clue looking like a verb the surface needs — release the prisoner — and it is an adjective about money instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Gratis means at no charge, so 'Free' is the price sense of the word rather than the liberty the surface is pushing.

clue.text: Private put in grave situation backed foreign ruler (8)

indicators.note: Something backed has been turned to face the other way, so an across piece is written from its last letter to its first.

blocks.note: to inter is to put a body in a grave; 'situation' fills out the picture without adding a letter
roi is French for king, and his three letters are set down right to left

explanation.surface: A private soldier in deep trouble who came out in support of a foreign king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' is the rank the whole surface is built on, and a crossword usually turns that into PTE or GI. Here it is not wordplay at all — it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Interior means inner, and a person's interior life is their private one, so the adjective substitutes directly.

clue.text: New missile limited in scope (6)

blocks.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
a missile is anything shot or thrown, not just the modern sort

explanation.surface: A new weapon with a disappointingly short range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missile' sounds like hardware from a defence budget and covers the oldest projectile there is, which is the whole distance the clue asks you to travel.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrow interests or a narrow outlook cover very little ground, which is what being limited in scope means of a person or a subject.

clue.text: Reluctantly agree about son’s intention (6)

indicators.note: About means round, so the letters of the piece named first open up and close again around what comes next.

blocks.note: to deign is to agree while making plain you are lowering yourself, and the word parts after its second letter
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A parent grudgingly going along with what a son means to do.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the sense in 'by design' or 'have designs on' — a purpose, not a pattern — and the surface's family argument is what keeps the drawing sense in your head.
explanation.definitionFit: To have designs on something is to intend to get it, so design is a plan or purpose rather than a drawing.

clue.text: Richard’s pronouncement on corporation, statement of principle (6)

indicators.note: A pronouncement is something spoken, so the name in front of it is wanted for the noise it makes rather than the way it is spelt.

blocks.note: Richard's familiar short form is Dick, and only the sound of it is wanted, so the hard closing letter is never written
a corporation is old comic English for a pot belly — a tum

explanation.surface: Richard delivering his verdict on some large company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' is the joke: not a company at all but the Victorian word for a paunch. Say the two halves one after the other and you are already saying the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dictum is a short formal saying that lays down a principle, the sort of line a judge or a critic is quoted for.

clue.text: Thing reversed in chart I revised as piece of mathematics (10)

indicators.note: Reversed says the piece is turned end for end, so an across entry takes those letters from the last to the first.
In means inside, so the turned-round piece is planted among the shuffled letters rather than set beside them.
Revising something means going back over it and altering it, so these letters will not stay in the order they are given.

blocks.note: six letters resettled into a new order, then parted to make room
a thing is an item, and these are its four letters read the other way round

explanation.surface: Something turned the wrong way round in a chart that had to be revised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chart I revised' reads as the setter talking about his own diagram, and the 'I' is nothing of the kind: it is one more letter of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Arithmetic is the branch of mathematics that deals with numbers and the four operations, so it is one part of the wider subject.

clue.text: Humble soldiers protecting area (4)

indicators.note: Troops protecting something close round it on all sides, so the letters of the first piece open and take the next inside.

blocks.note: the men are the ranks as against the officers, and the word parts after its second letter
A is the standard abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A guard of soldiers thrown round a patch of ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition wants a sense that has nearly died out — low in rank, as in mean streets or mean birth — while the two everyday senses, unkind and average, lead nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A man of mean birth is one of humble birth — the old sense of low in rank, not the modern unkind or average.

clue.text: These days, rarely fit for sports event (4)

blocks.note: fit in the old sense of proper or seemly, a use now confined to prayers and Shakespeare — which is what 'these days, rarely' is warning you about
an athletics or swimming fixture, where several clubs come together to compete

explanation.surface: A complaint that hardly anybody is in shape for athletics nowadays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'These days, rarely' is not an instruction but a usage label, telling you the first sense is archaic. The surface reads it as a remark about national fitness.
explanation.definitionFit: Meet is an old adjective for fitting or proper, and a meet is also the fixture at which athletes or swimmers compete.

clue.text: Stand-in to make score of ten, say (6)

blocks.note: the actor who replaces the star for the dangerous shots and the distant ones
a score is twenty, so making a score out of ten means multiplying it by two — and 'say' admits that any other number would do as well

explanation.surface: A substitute sent on with instructions to knock up ten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Score' looks like a total in a match, which is what a stand-in on the field suggests. It is the old counting word for twenty, as in four score and seven years ago.
explanation.definitionFit: A double is the stand-in who takes an actor's place, and to double ten is to turn it into twenty, which is a score.

clue.text: Something used by cooks in USA – pecan nuts (8)

indicators.note: Calling something nuts says it has gone haywire, and letters gone haywire are not in the order they arrived in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: American pecans going into whatever the cook has on the hob.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' has to be read as mad rather than as the pecans it is sitting beside, and the dash does nothing but keep the surface readable.
explanation.definitionFit: A saucepan is the deep pan with a long handle that a cook boils and simmers in, so the definition names it by who reaches for it.
